attributes.description: Every Kibana saved-object read and change, by type, name, space and actor.

params.markdown:
### Every change to your Kibana content, and who made it

Dashboards, visualizations, data views, alert rules, SLOs, workflows and other saved objects: what was created, edited, deleted or opened, in which space, and by whom.

Use it to answer questions such as "Who deleted that dashboard?" or "What changed before the alert stopped firing?" Panels marked *noise gate applied* skip these audit dashboards' own activity, so you see your team's work.

**How to use it:** choose a Project, Person (email) or Client IP in the controls and set the time picker. The session view at the bottom replays one browser session step by step. Click a session bar or a session ID to see exactly what happened in that browser session.

query.esql: FROM logs-elastic_cloud.serverless_audit.otel-* | WHERE @timestamp <= ?_tend AND @timestamp > ?_tstart | WHERE service.name == "serverless-kibana" | STATS `Kibana events` = COUNT(*)
FROM logs-elastic_cloud.serverless_audit.otel-* | WHERE @timestamp <= ?_tend AND @timestamp > ?_tstart | WHERE service.name == "serverless-kibana" | STATS `Kibana events` = COUNT(*)

embeddableConfig.description: All Kibana audit events. Usually a small fraction of raw stream volume, but most of the forensic value — this is where saved objects, spaces and sessions are recorded.

query.esql: FROM logs-elastic_cloud.serverless_audit.otel-* | WHERE @timestamp <= ?_tend AND @timestamp > ?_tstart | WHERE (service.name == "serverless-kibana" AND ((event.type IN ("change","creation","deletion") AND (event.action IS NULL OR NOT (event.action IN ("saved_object_open_point_in_time","saved_object_close_point_in_time")))) OR event.action IN ("rule_run_soon","secret_create"))) | STATS `Mutations` = COUNT(*)

embeddableConfig.description: Every Kibana state change in range, selected by ECS event.type rather than by an action-name suffix. That matters: a suffix test cannot see rule_enable, rule_disable, the whole case_user_action family, or anything the workflow, ML and agent-builder features emit, because none of those action names end in _create/_update/_delete. Point-in-time open/close are ECS-tagged creation/deletion but are query internals, and are excluded by name.

embeddableConfig.description: Distinct Kibana objects accessed or modified in range — reads included, as the name says. embeddableConfig.description: The single most important panel in the suite: state changes in Kibana, with who did it, what it was called, and which space it lives in. Each row groups the same change made again: one identity, one operation, one object, one space and one result over the whole time range. Events is how many times that happened and Last change is the newest of them, so a row reading Events 17 is seventeen changes, and the Mutations tile counts each one. The table holds the 30 groups changed most recently; every change in range is in "All mutations" on Security & Anomalies, and the "Kibana saved-object activity" session further down this page lists reads and changes together. Two columns to read carefully. Object type and Object are the real saved-object fields where Kibana records them and are otherwise recovered from the event message, because workflows, ML jobs and agent-builder objects carry no saved_object fields. A workflow cancel, or a test of an unsaved draft, names only its run, so it reads "execution" and the run id's first 8 characters. Result is "attempted" where Kibana logged the attempt rather than the outcome — that is how the saved-object path records things, so it is normal, and a "failure" here is a change that was denied. An Identity shown as “_4KEO… · Cloud API key” is an organization-level Elastic Cloud API key: the audit stream records it only by its opaque 20-character id, shown here by its first five characters; it has no name and no owner email. The table holds more rows than the panel shows: scroll it for the rest.
embeddableConfig.title: Mutations — most recent Kibana state changes, repeats grouped into one row · 30 at most

embeddableConfig.description: Saved-object type against operation, writes first; all Kibana traffic, reads included. Cell colour is the event count on a log scale, running teal (fewest) through blue and purple to pink (most); the legend spans exactly the counts drawn and labels both its ends. Every cell has an outline, so a single create, update or delete stays visible beside thousands of reads: the write columns are the forensic signal. An operation outside these words keeps Kibana's own, between the changes and the reads: "remove refs" (saved_object_remove_references) is a tag being unlinked from the objects it labelled, and it is one of the "other change" bars beside; "no action" is an event Kibana recorded without one (a Fleet policy deploy). Past 13 object types the rest share one "N more types" row at the bottom; types with any write rank first, so a rare change is never the one folded away. Hover a cell for its count and how many distinct objects it covers.
embeddableConfig.title: Object type × operation

embeddableConfig.description: The Mutations tile over time, by operation: the same events, so the bars add up to that tile. Creates, updates and deletes each have a colour; every other change — enabling, disabling, running, testing or cancelling a rule or workflow, opening or starting an ML job, removing references — is one "other change" series, because each is a few events a day and would be a sliver no one could see. The Mutations table above names each one. Reads are left out because they outnumber changes about thirty to one and flattened every change into a sliver; the heatmap beside this panel and the Object types table below show them. A deploy shows as a block of creates, updates and deletes together.
embeddableConfig.title: Kibana state changes over time · reads in the heatmap

embeddableConfig.description: One row per object: its title from kibana.saved_object.name, or its id where Kibana recorded no title (a space); two objects with the same title (one dashboard installed in two spaces) are told apart by the id after the title, and a renamed object is one row under one of its titles. The advanced-settings object, whose id is the Kibana version, reads "Advanced settings 9.6.0" — one per space, counted together — and a usage counter (Kibana's per-object view count) leads with the object it counts. Ranked by events, reads and changes together. embeddableConfig.description: Kibana events that named an object, reads and changes, newest first; the newest 1,000 in range, so the result count above the grid is that cap, not a total. Like the two tables above: behind the noise gate, as on Command Center's Live signal feed: it leaves out what the gate calls query internals — views of this audit suite's own dashboards, searches and data view, the suite's automated install (the API imports, exports and writes that deploy it, with no browser session), the settings and data-view lookups every Kibana page load makes, space lookups and point-in-time paging — which otherwise filled every row with the suite watching and installing itself. It is a test of what happened, never of who or where: creating or deleting a space and everything Kibana deletes along with it (its settings, usage counters and the objects in it), and test or probe objects, stay, the suite's own review tooling included, because they are real changes. A usage counter's Object leads with the object it counts. A suite object a person changed in Kibana is kept; every change, the install's included, is in Mutations at the top of the page. Kibana's page requests and logins name no object and are left out too. Object is the title the object had when the event was recorded, so a renamed object shows its old title on older rows; the id in Message does not change. embeddableConfig.description: One bar per Kibana browser session in the last 24 hours, newest first — its length runs from the first to the last thing they did in it and its strength is how much it did, which are independent: a short session can carry far more activity than a long one left open and idle. Click a bar to filter the dashboard to that session (a "session: …" pill on kibana.session.id) and to set the time range to the session plus a minute either side, so the session records directly below this timeline show exactly that session's events: those records follow the time picker, while this timeline stays on its fixed 24 hours. To return, remove the pill and set the time range again. The pill narrows every panel on the page to that session, so a panel of Elasticsearch events, which carry no session id, reads empty while it is on. Shift-click pins that identity by email across the suite instead. What an open browser tab does on its own — internal page requests, usage counters, point-in-time paging — is left out, exactly as in the session records below, so a tab left open does not stretch a bar past the person's last action and every bar has records under it. Only Kibana browser sign-ins carry a session id: work through an API key or the Elasticsearch API has no session and draws no bar, so the dashed line marks the latest such event in the same 24 hours — activity after the last bar is real, it is just not a session. An identity that only works through the API has no bars, and that is the correct answer. Twelve most recent sessions, each labelled with who and when it started (with the weekday when that was not today); a session already open when the 24-hour window begins starts at the window's left edge and is labelled "or earlier", because its real start is outside the window. Times are in your browser's timezone, like the rest of Kibana. Fixed 24-hour window: does not follow the time picker.
embeddableConfig.title: Kibana browser sessions · fixed last 24 hours, your time zone

embeddableConfig.description: One person's Kibana sessions, event by event, newest first: every object they opened and changed, with the sentence Kibana wrote for each, which names the object's type and id ("User has resolved dashboard [id=…]"). Operation uses the same words as the heatmap (get, resolve, create …); an event that names no object keeps its own action, such as "http request" for a public API call. To replay one session, click its bar in the session timeline above (it pins that session and zooms the time range to it), or hover a cell of the kibana.session.id column and choose Filter for value; then open in Discover and sort Time ascending to read it forward. Kibana's internal UI requests, usage counters, space lookups and point-in-time internals are left out; public API calls such as an export are kept, and so are views of this audit suite, because they are part of what the person did. That is why the panel can be empty while Cross-space activity above counts a signed-in person: a browser tab left open keeps sending those background requests (tag lists, usage counters, paging) without the person opening or changing anything. Object is the title the object had at the time, so a renamed object shows its old title on older rows. The session column keeps its field name, kibana.session.id, because a Discover session takes a header only from a rename, and a renamed column offers no Filter for on a dashboard; it holds the full id, cut to fit, and expanding a row (the expand control at its left) shows all of it. On a narrow screen the grid scrolls sideways for Space and Message. API-key traffic carries no session. An Identity shown as “_4KEO… · Cloud API key” is an organization-level Elastic Cloud API key: the audit stream records it only by its opaque 20-character id, shown here by its first five characters; it has no name and no owner email. This panel is empty when no browser session opened or changed anything.
embeddableConfig.title: Session reconstruction · newest 1,000 at most (empty when no browser session opened or changed anything)
